papers.title: When Agentic Retrieval Fails Silently: Framework and Production Evidence from a Creative AI Assistant
papers.authors: Yan, Liang, Anuj Agarwal, Aditya Reddy Cheruku
papers.abstract: CTR, MRR, and behavioral NDCG assume the user sees ranked results and acts on them. In an agentic assistant, a generation layer consumes retrieval output first, and that assumption breaks in three ways. The agent reads the results before the user does (who). The user's action can come several turns or sessions after retrieval (when). Outcomes blend retrieved content with the model's own knowledge (what caused it). We call this the attribution gap. We propose Layered Agentic Retrieval Assessment (LARA), which measures retrieval quality, engagement and outcome, and product success as three independent layers joined by a four-field lineage schema that requires no new modeling. We examine the motivation on Adobe Express, where one retrieval infrastructure serves a gallery search surface and an agentic assistant at roughly one-eighth its session volume for the same user population. Chat users reformulate more than gallery users (44.4% vs. 33.1%) because chat reformulation refines generated output. LARA restores attribution for the retrieval.

deep_reading.title: When Agentic Retrieval Fails Silently: Framework and Production Evidence from a Creative AI Assistant
deep_reading.content:
Adobe Express's template gallery search and its AI assistant run on the same retrieval system and serve the same users. Intuition says assistant users don't look at result lists, so they should reformulate queries less. In fact the chat entry point has a reformulation rate of 44.4%, against 33.1% for the gallery, 11 points higher. The reason is that "reformulation" means different things on the two sides. In the gallery, a user reformulates because the results were irrelevant and they try other words. In chat, most reformulations come after the user sees a generated result and wants to tweak it, such as "a bit bluer" or "use a bolder font". More surprising still, ==the assistant actually called retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts==. The three Adobe authors call this the **attribution gap**: CTR, MRR and behavioral NDCG all assume the user saw a ranked list and acted on it, and in an AI assistant that assumption breaks in three directions at once. The paper's evaluation framework, LARA, uses three independent layers of measurement plus four log fields to give credit back to retrieval, without training any new model.

## 1. The problem: the agent reads first, the user comes later

The authors argue that the failure comes from three structural changes, none of which tuning can fix.

The first change is who looks at the results. In the gallery, a user searches "birthday invitation", scrolls through 40 templates and clicks one, and that click is a grade for retrieval. In the assistant, the user says they want a birthday invitation, a search sub-agent retrieves templates, and the agent picks one and turns it straight into a design; the user never sees the other 39. There may be no click at all, and what the user does see has already been filtered and reordered by the agent.

The second change is that action takes longer to arrive. The same asset may be retrieved in turn 1 and again in turn 3, and only exported in turn 5 or even in another session. The logs have no identifier linking that export to a particular retrieval, so timing alone cannot tell which retrieval deserves the credit.

The third change is that nobody can say what caused the outcome. When the result is bad, there is no way to tell whether retrieval or generation went wrong. When the result is good, the model may have quietly made up for a failed retrieval.

![Paper Table 1: the assumption each of the three structural shifts breaks, how existing metrics mislead, and LARA's corresponding fix.](figs/2610.30423/crop_tab1.png)

Without per-component instrumentation, teams can only watch session-level signals such as retries, abandonment and task completion. The authors point out that retries alone go wrong in both directions. They fire when generation fails for reasons that have nothing to do with retrieval, and they stay silent when the model covers for retrieval. That third case is the most dangerous, because in session-level signals it looks exactly like success.

## 2. Method: measure where a problem is first visible

LARA's principle is to measure each component's failures at the earliest point where they can be seen. So it has three layers; the higher the layer, the closer it is to product outcomes and the more it depends on the lineage fields described later.

![Paper Figure 1: LARA's three layers. Layer 1 can be computed from server-side logs alone; Layers 2 and 3 rely on the lineage fields that run through all three layers on the right.](figs/2610.30423/crop_fig1.png)

Layer 1 asks only about retrieval itself: did the sub-agent return the right assets in the right order? The metrics are null rate, precision@1, precision@K and NDCG@K, computed at the moment retrieval fires from server-side logs with offline relevance labels (human or LLM judge), independent of what the user or agent does afterwards. CTR serves here only as a secondary directional signal. Only this layer can catch a retrieval failure that the model has masked.

Layer 2 asks whether what came back was actually used, and whether there are signs that retrieval was wrong. This layer counts positive evidence and failure evidence separately and reports them by "retrieval role". The retrieval role is written to the log at retrieval time and says what the retrieval was for: finding something directly, finding something to look at, finding something to act on, serving as a reference input for generation, being one step in a larger task, or depending on context. The layer has four metrics:

- **Genuine positive rate (GPR)**: the share of retrievals where, after the results were shown to the user, the user actively used a returned asset, for example by asking a follow-up about it, or by selecting, editing or exporting it.
- **Agent consumption rate (ACR)**: the share of retrievals where the agent used a returned asset within the same request, before the user received anything, for example when a user asks in one sentence for a logo with the background removed. This also counts as positive evidence, but it is tracked separately, because it reflects only the agent's judgment; the user's later action is the independent confirmation.
- **Observable retrieval failure rate (ORF)**: the share of retrievals followed by one of three retrieval-specific signals. The first is the user saying the retrieved object or path is wrong. The second is searching again for the same unresolved need. The third is the agent using something else when the flow should have used the returned asset. When the user keeps the asset and only modifies the edit or the generated result, that is a "downstream correction" and does not count as a retrieval failure. 1−ORF should be reported alongside GPR and ACR, but it must not be treated as satisfaction.
- **Unobserved outcome rate (UOR)**: the share of retrievals with neither evidence of use nor a failure signal. It is its own category, counted as neither abandonment nor success.

Layer 3 asks whether the user reached their goal. In a creative tool the clearest signals are export, share and download. Task completion is defined per retrieval role, and whether the goal was reached needs an LLM judge or human labels. Only when these success events can be linked back, through the lineage fields, to the retrieval that supplied the asset does this layer become a signal about retrieval; otherwise it only reflects overall product health.

## 3. Read two layers together, then add four log fields

Reading Layer 1 and Layer 2 side by side tells you which component went wrong:

| Layer 1 | Layer 2 | Diagnosis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low | High ORF | Retrieval returned the wrong assets |
| High | Low ORF, many downstream corrections | Assets were fine; generation failed |
| High | High ORF (agent rejection) | The agent bypassed good results (parametric knowledge leaking in) |
| Low | ORF near zero | A silent retrieval failure masked by the model |

The last row is the most dangerous. Without Layer 1 this failure is completely invisible; with Layer 1 it shows up the moment retrieval fires, with no need to wait for user complaints to pile up.

For Layers 2 and 3 to work, the logs must be able to link actions back to retrievals. Today Adobe's production logs have no field shared by retrieval events and action events, and the authors propose four fields to close the gap. The first is a unique `retrieval_id` on every retrieval. The second is `returned_asset_ids`, the full ranked list at the moment retrieval fires, recorded before the generation layer filters or reorders it; this field alone makes Layer 1 computable, so it is the single change with the best payoff. The third is a `consumed_asset_id` on every action event, whether the action comes from the user or from an agent tool call. The fourth is a `source_retrieval_id` on the same event, pointing to the retrieval that supplied the asset; for an asset already placed in the document, the field is inherited from the placement event.

All four are additions to logging, not predictive models. Because `source_retrieval_id` points to a retrieval rather than a session, attribution stays clear even when the same asset is retrieved again over several turns or exported in a new session. Together the four fields can also recover the rank of the asset that was actually used within the retrieval results, independent of the order finally shown to the user. That lets RAG evaluation frameworks such as RAGAs and ARES use direct attribution instead of guessing from timing.

One example ties the four fields together. A user says in chat, "Find a birthday invitation template and change the title to Xiaoming's 6th birthday." The retrieval event records `retrieval_id=r1` and 20 candidates. The agent picks the fourth one and changes the title; this is an agent event carrying `consumed_asset_id` and `source_retrieval_id=r1`, and it counts toward ACR. Two days later the user exports from the editor, and the export event inherits r1, counting as a "retrieval-attributed export" in Layer 3. Without these fields, the export would land in another session and the original chat session would be counted as abandoned.

## 4. Production data from Adobe Express

The authors analyzed production sessions from August 2026. LARA's lineage fields are not live yet, so every "was it used" number below is inferred from timing. Session, user and query counts are withheld under Adobe's disclosure policy; the paper says only that gallery volume is roughly 8–9 times the assistant's.

![Paper Table 3: Adobe Express, August 2026, traditional behavioral metrics for gallery search versus the AI assistant on the same retrieval infrastructure and user population.](figs/2610.30423/crop_tab3.png)

The data confirms the points from Section 1 in three ways. The first is that the agent reads first. The assistant's overall CTR is close to zero because 99.7% of interactions never called retrieval at all, so there is not even a denominator. When retrieval does fire, it behaves normally: the null rate is 1.51%, and users click about 1.05 times per returned result grid. Testing directly whether the agent used the results would need ACR, which cannot be computed yet.

The second is delayed action. Assistant sessions average 2.04 prompts, and the chat entry point averages 2.65, with the same asset reappearing in later turns. An export started from chat is logged under a different `session_guid` once the user leaves the chat interface. Session-level attribution then counts those users as abandoning, so the chat abandonment rate (59.5%) is overstated and engagement is understated.

The third is that retrieval and generation are mixed together. The reformulation inversion from the opening is the example: one behavioral signal mixes retrieval failures with tweaks to generated results, so the aggregate number says nothing. LARA splits it in two: "search reformulation", counted only on retrieval turns, and "downstream correction", counted on the other turns.

With current logs, the team can compute only the null rate and clicks per grid today. Precision@K and NDCG@K also need `returned_asset_ids` and a labeled sample. GPR, ACR, ORF and UOR need the other three fields plus the retrieval role, and for now can only be obtained by labeling traces by hand. In other words, the team can confirm that retrieval works when it fires, but cannot yet confirm whether the user or the agent actually used what came back.

## 5. A surprise: retrieval is almost never called

Gallery search is retrieval by definition, while the assistant called retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts; about 82% of assistant activity is generative editing with no corresponding search scenario at all. The authors think the bigger risk may be **missed retrieval**: the planner routes "help me find a birthday invitation template" to generative editing, no retrieval event is created, and Layer 1 has nothing to score. Table 3 shows 10.7% of chat prompts with retrieval intent; this number is only directional. But if it does reflect intent rather than actual triggering, the gap between it and 0.31% is a first estimate of missed retrieval.

The authors call planner routing Layer 0 and treat it as an extension of LARA rather than a fourth layer. It has two metrics. The misroute rate is the share of retrieval calls whose prompt was not actually in scope for retrieval; those calls should be removed from Layer 1. The missed-retrieval rate is the share of prompts with retrieval intent that did not trigger retrieval, which needs ground-truth intent labels. In a sample of 273 prompts, about 5–7% contained two or more distinct retrieval intents, so routing also has to be able to split multi-intent requests.

## 6. Limitations and practical value

The limitations the authors list are concrete. All the evidence comes from one deployment, and the 0.31% figure and the reformulation inversion may be specific to a creative assistant dominated by generative editing. None of the lineage fields is live, so every Layer 2 number is inferred from timing, and the retrieval roles were inferred after the fact rather than recorded at retrieval time. The chat abandonment rate is overstated by cross-session exports. The data was not validated for schema or value ranges, and synthetic traffic was removed by hand. Latency and tokens per successful task were not instrumented by stage either. LARA covers only the retrieval component; how the agent understands intent, generates queries and splits multi-intent requests needs separate instrumentation. This is a short industry paper, and the framework has not been validated across multiple deployments or in online experiments.

The authors' three lessons for practitioners are useful. First, ==do not use the assistant's overall CTR or reformulation rate as retrieval metrics==: retrieval metrics should be counted only on turns where retrieval fired, and reformulations should be split into search reformulations and downstream corrections. Second, start by logging the full ranked list when retrieval fires; only this field makes Layer 1 computable. Third, define "the user actively used it" once and publish the definition: in Express chat, the effective action rate ranges from 7.6% to 40.5% depending on which behaviors are counted, so without a shared definition the numbers cannot be compared. For teams embedding search into an agent, the paper's biggest reminder is that when retrieval is called on only 0.31% of prompts, the question is not only whether it ranks well, but whether it gets called at all.

papers.title: AutoSim: A Self-Improving User Simulator for Conversational Search Evaluation
papers.authors: Saber Zerhoudi, Jelena Mitrovic, Michael Granitzer
papers.abstract: User simulators promise to evaluate conversational search systems at a scale human studies cannot reach, but only if their behavior is realistic enough to trust. We study AutoSim, a conversational-search user simulator whose relevance judgments rank a controlled pool of retrieval systems in agreement with NIST across three TREC iKAT years (Kendall's $τ$ of $0.66$, $0.91$, and $0.91$; all $p{\le}0.002$), an agreement that survives removing its persona. AutoSim self-improves against a held-out signal from real users, and we find that fine-tuning its weights makes it behave like real users, which in turn gives a more accurate estimate of how well a system serves them. Reaching that behavior takes more than prompting: when discriminating between real and simulated user sessions, no prompt we tried lowers a held-out real-versus-simulated classifier below AUC $0.85$, whereas fine-tuning the weights drives it to $0.45$, where neither the classifier nor a human reading full dialogues can tell it from a real user. That added realism is what makes the evaluation more accurate: where real users retrieve little, a prompted simulator over-estimates retrieval effectiveness by $+0.136$ nDCG and returns a relevant passage on $57\%$ of the turns where real users find none, enough to change a deployment decision. Only the weight-level simulator escapes this bias. We release the framework and code.
papers.summary: Conversational search needs trustworthy user simulators for scale. AutoSim’s relevance judgments rank a controlled pool of retrieval systems in agreement with NIST across three TREC iKAT years (Kendall τ 0.66 / 0.91 / 0.91, all p≤0.002), and that agreement survives removing its persona. Self-improving against held-out real-user signal, weight-level self-improvement drives real-vs-sim AUC from ~0.85 down to 0.45, lifts retrieval +0.136 nDCG, and returns a relevant passage on 57% of turns. ==A simulator is trustworthy when it ranks systems like NIST, not when it merely sounds human==.

deep_reading.title: AutoSim: A Self-Improving User Simulator for Conversational Search Evaluation
deep_reading.content:
Ask a strong LLM to play a search user and it writes 37.5 words per message on average, while real users write only 12.8. A discriminator that never saw the training data recognizes its utterances with AUC 0.88, and the passages its queries retrieve barely overlap with those of real users (overlap@5 is only 0.01). The conversational search user simulator AutoSim, studied in this SIGIR-AP 2026 paper, is in exactly this state: its rankings of retrieval systems agree with NIST in three TREC iKAT years (Kendall τ of 0.66, 0.91 and 0.91), yet the way it talks is far from human. The authors constrain the simulator's self-improvement with held-out real-user data, and the conclusion is clear: ==changing only the prompt cannot push discriminator AUC below 0.85; changing the model weights brings AUC down to 0.45==, to the point that people reading whole conversations cannot tell. More importantly, sounding human changes evaluation conclusions. Where real users retrieve poorly, a prompt-driven simulator overestimates nDCG by 0.136, enough to change a launch decision.

![Real-vs-simulated discriminator AUC on held-out iKAT for four simulator configurations: default prompt, tuned prompt, few-shot prompt and weight-level fine-tuning (AutoSim); 0.5 means indistinguishable.](figs/2610.28054/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: can a simulator be trusted, and what should change to make it more human?

With a user simulator, a conversational search system does not need a human study for every design change, and tuning a ranker or a clarifying-question policy can be compared reproducibly. But the simulator's persona, prompts and rules are fixed at design time, and when the system under evaluation changes, the simulator does not change with it. Prior work also found that it is unreliable in itself: swapping only the underlying user model swings the evaluated agent's task success rate by about 9 percentage points, and general LLM simulators systematically overestimate success. And a more human-like simulator is not necessarily a more accurate evaluator.

The authors therefore ask three questions. First, can AutoSim rank retrieval systems the way NIST does? Second, can self-improvement narrow its behavioral gap with real people, and should it change the prompt or the weights? Third, once the gap narrows, is it a better evaluator? The authors first run a diagnosis and find that the default simulator's relevance judgments already agree with NIST; the gap lies in "what the user says and asks", and changing the generation prompt cannot close it. So the overall design is: leave the relevance judge untouched and rewrite only the utterance generator, at the weight level.

## 2. Method: AutoSim and its self-improvement loop

![AutoSim drives a real conversational search system: the loop records simulator trajectories and proposes edits, and only edits that do not regress on a held-out set are accepted; the editable components are the relevance-judgment instructions and the utterance generator.](figs/2610.28054/hf2.png)

The other is the utterance generator, the model that writes what the simulated user says; it can be changed through its prompt or its parameters, and this is the core comparison of the paper.

The communication-style part is measured in two ways. One looks at statistics such as average word count, the share of polite phrasing and the share of very short messages; these are easy to read and also easy to write directly into a prompt. The other trains a discriminator on held-out data to tell real utterances from simulated ones and reports ROC AUC, with 0.5 meaning indistinguishable. The latter is an adversarial standard that cannot be passed by matching a few numbers. As we will see, the two measures reach different conclusions, and that is itself a result.

Each round of the self-improvement loop first records the simulator's full trajectory, including what action it chose each turn, what it retrieved, what it clicked and what it said. It then clusters the differences between simulated and real behavior into a few groups, has a model from a different family than the generator write an evaluator for each group, and proposes candidate edits with reflective population search. Only edits that do not regress on a calibration set are accepted, while a rolling held-out set is also monitored.

The weight-level change is more direct. The authors first LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B on real iKAT utterances as a starting point, then run 4 rounds of adversarial rejection sampling: each round generates several candidate utterances for each held-out turn, keeps the ones the frozen discriminator considers most human, fine-tunes further on them, and retrains the discriminator.

| --- | ---: |
| None (default prompt) | 0.88 |
| Prompt level (best of four methods) | 0.84 |
| Weight level, LoRA starting point on real data | 0.45 |

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Default (verbose) | 28 | +0.136 | +0.009 |
| Terse prompt | 9 | +0.087 | −0.028 |
| Length-matched truncation | 11 | +0.071 | −0.042 |
| Weight level | 12 | +0.014 | +0.015 |

papers.title: Learning Marginal Viewpoint Utility for Budgeted Evidence Selection in RAG
papers.authors: Yiyang Duan, Ziqi Yu, Tiantong Wu, Yebo Wu, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over multi-viewpoint queries must preserve distinct answers and positions from the retrieved evidence while operating under a fixed context budget. We introduce LMVU, a lightweight ranker that learns to prioritize candidates by the marginal viewpoint coverage they add to the current selection. Training uses viewpoint annotations from each benchmark's development split to compare candidates within the same selection state. At inference, LMVU repeatedly scores budget-feasible candidates as the context grows, without accessing these annotations. We evaluate two forms of recovered viewpoint coverage: RVC$_1$ assigns each viewpoint full credit for at least one supporting source unit, while RVC$_2$ assigns half credit for one and full credit for two or more distinct source units. Exact oracles measure achievable coverage under the same evidence pool and budget. Across four viewpoint-annotated benchmarks at a 1,024-token budget, LMVU achieves gains of up to 0.047 and 0.052 points in RVC$_1$ and RVC$_2$, respectively, over the strongest non-oracle baseline for each benchmark and metric, and reaches the exact viewpoint-breadth ceiling on two benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multi-viewpoint RAG must keep distinct answers and stances under a fixed context budget. LMVU ranks by the marginal viewpoint coverage a candidate adds to the current selection, trained with viewpoint annotations that compare candidates in the same selection state, and rescoring budget-feasible candidates as context grows. It reaches 94.6% coverage on Perspectrum and matches or nears full coverage on WVS/ESS10, beating the strongest baselines. ==For multi-viewpoint retrieval, rank by marginal coverage, not per-doc relevance alone==.

deep_reading.content:
Ask a question about election participation, and a complete answer should cover three kinds of people: those who voted, those who did not, and those who were not eligible; if the context holds only voters' answers, it represents only one viewpoint, however accurate and relevant each one is. Under a 1024-token context budget, classic MMR repeatedly selects evidence supporting the same three viewpoints on a corruption-perception query from the World Values Survey (WVS), and misses the viewpoint "there is no corruption". This paper from Nanyang Technological University and the University of Toronto proposes LMVU (learned marginal viewpoint utility), a linear ranker with only 18 coefficients that picks evidence by "how many not-yet-covered viewpoints this piece adds to the current context". The authors evaluate with recall viewpoint coverage (RVC, the fraction of annotated viewpoints the context covers). On four viewpoint-annotated benchmarks, ==LMVU reaches the same full coverage as the exact optimum on the protected WVS test fold, and averages RVC 0.9588 across the four benchmarks, beating all 16 non-oracle methods==, including two neural rerankers that cost orders of magnitude more to train.

![(a) Evidence selected for a WVS corruption-perception query under the same candidate pool and a 1024-token budget: MMR covers 3 viewpoints, while LMVU adds the "no corruption" viewpoint to cover all 4; (b) the average viewpoint-coverage gap between MMR and the exact full-pool optimum on each benchmark.](figs/2610.29234/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: relevant is not the same as covering

RAG usually ranks passages by relevance to the query and puts the relevant ones into the context first. But some queries need coverage of different answers or stances. The authors call "an answer category or stance supported by a set of evidence" a viewpoint. Highly relevant evidence may all support the same viewpoint, leaving other viewpoints unrepresented. Methods like MMR trade off relevance against "how similar this is to already selected evidence", and recent diversity-seeking RAG selection methods follow the same idea. But semantic diversity is not viewpoint coverage: evidence worded differently can support the same viewpoint, and evidence worded similarly can take opposite stances.

The authors frame the task as a coverage problem under a budget. Each query has a full candidate pool and an annotated list of viewpoints; each piece of evidence has its own token cost and supports some of those viewpoints. The goal is to have the selected evidence cover as many viewpoints as possible while total cost stays within budget, counting each viewpoint once, and this fraction is RVC. The key constraint is that annotations are invisible at inference: viewpoint labels are used only for training and evaluation, and the selector can only estimate how many new viewpoints the next piece of evidence will bring from visible evidence features and what has already been selected. Because labels are available at evaluation, the authors can compute the exact full-pool optimum with dynamic programming, and so measure how far any selection method is from the optimum, which they call headroom.

## 2. Method: learning each piece of evidence's marginal viewpoint utility

![LMVU overview: (a) on the development set, gold marginal gains are used to build within-state preference pairs that train a linear scorer; (b) at inference, without labels, it greedily selects among budget-feasible candidates and rescores after each step.](figs/2610.29234/hf2.png)

What the selector really needs at each step is a candidate's marginal gain given the current selection, that is, how many not-yet-covered viewpoints it fills in. The same candidate's gain changes as the selection changes, and once all the viewpoints it supports are covered, its gain drops to zero. This gain requires labels to compute, so it cannot be used in deployment, but it can be computed on the development set, so the authors use it to train a surrogate scorer that imitates it using only features visible at inference.

The training data comes from the following procedure. On a fixed development candidate pool, the authors make selections with five strategies: greedy by dense relevance, live MMR, two fixed-seed random orders, and greedy by true gain. Each selection run is cut into at most its first 9 steps, giving many "half-selected" states; after removing duplicates, they take up to 20 candidates per state and compute each one's true gain from the labels.

The scorer itself is a linear combination of 18 features. The features fall into four groups: descriptions of the candidate itself, the geometric relation between the evidence and the selected set, the geometric relation between finer-grained atomic pieces and the selected set, and features describing the selected set as a whole. All similarities reuse the frozen embeddings already computed for dense retrieval, so no new model is needed. The last group of features is identical for all candidates in the same state, so it cancels out in comparisons and its fitted coefficients come out exactly zero; the budget therefore acts only through "does it fit", not through the score.

The authors do not regress the gain directly, because the range of gains differs across states, anywhere from zero to the number of viewpoints still uncovered. They compare only in pairs within the same state: if candidate A's true gain is larger than B's, the scorer must give A a higher score; tied pairs are dropped, and the model is fit with an L2-regularized pairwise logistic loss. Comparing this way cancels each state's own overall offset, and what gets optimized is exactly the decision the selector faces at each step. This differs from MMR in that MMR uses a fixed λ to trade off relevance and novelty; LMVU's weights are also fixed at inference, but they act on geometric features that update with the selection, so the novelty penalty changes with what has already been covered. The same candidate may rank high early on, and once its viewpoints are covered by other evidence, its rank drops.

Inference starts from an empty context. At each step it picks the highest-scoring candidate among those that fit entirely in the remaining budget, adds it and updates the state; when no candidate fits, it stops, and it never truncates evidence. Each step needs only one 18-dimensional dot product per candidate, maintained with incremental statistics, without building a similarity matrix over the whole pool. The authors also state plainly that LMVU only guarantees the selected set stays within budget, not how close its coverage is to the optimum.

## 3. Setup

The authors use four benchmarks. Two come from social surveys: the World Values Survey (WVS) and the European Social Survey Round 10 (ESS10). Perspectrum has a "claim plus different perspectives" structure, and ArgKP has an "argument plus key points" structure; the authors use it as a control where coverage is already saturated. These benchmarks vary widely in size, with average candidate pools ranging from 9 to 507 items, and evaluation queries are few: WVS and ArgKP have only 6 each. Budgets are 512, 1024 and 2048 tokens, with 1024 for the main results. WVS evaluation uses a protected respondent fold that is used only for pre-declared evaluation and read-only audits, never for fitting. The encoder is a frozen local all-MiniLM-L6-v2.

Besides breadth RVC, the authors report a "repeated support" version, RVC₂: a viewpoint supported by only one source scores half, and only two or more distinct sources score full, to measure depth. RAG usually ranks passages by relevance to the query and puts the relevant ones into the context first. But some queries need coverage of different answers or stances. But semantic diversity is not viewpoint coverage: evidence worded differently can support the same viewpoint, and evidence worded similarly can take opposite stances.

The authors frame the task as a coverage problem under a budget. Because labels are available at evaluation, the authors can compute the exact full-pool optimum with dynamic programming, and so measure how far any selection method is from the optimum, which they call headroom.

What the selector really needs at each step is a candidate's marginal gain given the current selection, that is, how many not-yet-covered viewpoints it fills in. This gain requires labels to compute, so it cannot be used in deployment, but it can be computed on the development set, so the authors use it to train a surrogate scorer that imitates it using only features visible at inference.

papers.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
papers.authors: Yang Liu, Zhiqiang Yuan, Shu-Dong Huang, Jiancheng Lv, Liwei Yang, Qiwei Yan, Kailin Lv, Jinchao Zhang
papers.abstract: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.
papers.summary: Embedding and generation are usually separate specialists with incompatible objectives; unified models like GritLM either switch attention regimes or train the two as parallel losses. ULME proposes predictive coupling so embedding and language modeling reinforce each other—aimed at RAG/agent pipelines that embed then generate the same query. ==Unifying embed+generate is about objective coupling, not shared weights plus a mode switch==.

deep_reading.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
deep_reading.content:
In RAG, in-context example selection and agent memory, the same query usually goes through two models: an embedding model first encodes it into a vector for retrieval, and then a generation model reads it again to answer. The two models are trained separately, and their understanding of the same query never connects. The authors, from Tencent WeChat AI and Sichuan University, argue that to write a coherent answer, a generation model's hidden states must already contain an "answer-relevant understanding of the query", which is exactly what a good embedding should have. They propose ULME, a post-training framework: insert a chain of learnable slots after the query in a causal decoder, then use a loss with a stop-gradient so that information from the generation side shapes the embedding in turn. Across 8 scales from 0.5B to 8B in the Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 families, ==a single ULME checkpoint beats the strongest open-source baseline on the same backbone by 3.3–4.1 points on MTEB==, while matching or beating generation-only fine-tuned models on MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro and HumanEval.

## 1. The problem: existing "unified models" only unify parameters

Turning an LLM into an embedding model is well established. E5-Mistral and NV-Embed fine-tune a causal LLM with contrastive learning and take the hidden state of the last token; LLM2Vec goes further and removes the causal mask, turning the model into a bidirectional encoder. They showed that decoder hidden states are enough for very strong embeddings, but the fine-tuned model can no longer be used for generation.

Putting retrieval and generation into one model has been tried too. GritLM trains one LLM on a contrastive loss and a language-modeling loss at the same time; another method, GEM, adds embedding ability to a generation model through extra tokens and self-supervised contrastive learning. The authors argue that these approaches unify only half the way, with gaps in two places.

The first gap is in the mechanism. GritLM switches to bidirectional attention for embedding and back to causal attention for generation, so what the embedding reads out is not on the same computation path as the hidden states used for generation.

The second gap is in the training objectives. The two losses train side by side on shared parameters without supervising each other: generation does not depend on the learned embedding, and the embedding receives no direct signal from the generation side. Sharing parameters does not by itself connect the two.

There is also a more concrete conflict about which position the embedding is read from. The usual way to embed with a causal LLM is to take the hidden state of the query's last token, but in a unified model that very position is responsible for predicting the first token of the answer. The authors call this a **representation conflict**: retrieval needs a sequence-level state that can be compared with other states by inner product, while language modeling needs a state that feeds the LM head and only cares about the next word, and one hidden state is asked to do both jobs.

## 2. Method: a chain of slots and three losses

![ULME overview: one causal decoder trains three objectives on a shared chain of learnable slots: semantic contrast, answer generation, and predictive coupling with a stop-gradient.](figs/2610.30705/hf1.png)

ULME's first step is to give the embedding its own readout positions. Borrowing from latent chain-of-thought methods such as Coconut and pause tokens, it inserts $N$ learnable slots between the query $q$ and the answer $a$, so a training sample reads $q\,\|\,\langle\textsc{emb}\rangle_{1:N}\,\|\,a$, while a document is encoded as $d\,\|\,\langle\textsc{emb}\rangle$. The slots are ordinary positions in the causal forward pass: each slot sees the query and earlier slots, and every answer token sees all slots. The mask is not changed at all and there are no side paths; attention is causal throughout, and one forward pass yields both the embedding and the answer. The first slot (slot 0) serves as the **semantic embedding**, and the last slot (slot $N-1$) as the **reasoning embedding**.

Training uses three losses at once. The first two are standard. One is a symmetric InfoNCE between the query representation and the document representation at slot 0, with in-batch negatives gathered across GPUs. The other is ordinary next-token cross-entropy, computed only on the answer. The slots themselves carry no token loss, but the slot chain sits on the causal path that produces the answer, so language-modeling gradients flow back into the slots through the answer's attention to them.

The authors point out that these two losses alone are exactly the "train side by side" setup of earlier unified models. The semantic loss only pulls slot 0 toward documents and ignores what the answer says; the generation loss is conditioned on the slots but never asks any slot to represent anything in particular.

So ULME adds a third loss, called predictive coupling, which builds a bridge between the two sides. It aligns the hidden state of the last query-side slot, $h_q^{(N-1)}$, with a pooling $r_{qa}$ of the answer's hidden states from the same forward pass (the mean by default). The alignment uses a one-directional in-batch InfoNCE with a stop-gradient ${\rm sg}(\cdot)$ on the answer side:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}=-\log\frac{\exp(\langle h_q^{(N-1)},{\rm sg}(r_{qa})\rangle/\tau)}{\sum_k\exp(\langle h_q^{(N-1)},{\rm sg}(r_{qa,k})\rangle/\tau)}$$

Putting the stop-gradient on the answer side is deliberate. $r_{qa}$ has seen both the query and the answer, so it holds more information than $h_q^{(N-1)}$, which has seen only the query and the slots; the side with less information should reach toward the side with more. If gradients also flowed back into $r_{qa}$, the answer-side representation would be pushed toward being "easy to tell apart within the batch", interfering with the hidden states the generation loss is supervising. In effect, the answer-side representation is distilled one way into query slots that are available at inference time. The three losses are summed with weights $\lambda_{\text{sem}}=\lambda_{\text{gen}}=1.0$ and $\lambda_{\text{pred}}=0.3$, and $N=4$ by default.

An example shows what each loss is responsible for. The query is "how do I deduplicate a Python list while keeping order", and the training answer is a snippet using `dict.fromkeys` plus an explanation. The semantic loss pulls slot 0 toward the embedding of the matching document; predictive coupling pulls slot 3 toward the mean of that answer's hidden states. At inference time there is no need to generate an answer: running the query plus 4 slots is enough to read out the embedding.

## 3. Embedding results

On the embedding side the training data is E5 contrastive data in LLM2Vec format; on the generation side it is OpenThoughts-114k. Each configuration is trained once and the final checkpoint is reported; at evaluation time no capability is switched off and no head is fine-tuned separately. Baseline numbers come from the LLM2VEC-GEN paper's reports on the same backbones.

**MTEB(eng, v2) average:**

| Backbone | LLM2Vec | LLM2VEC-GEN | ULME |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 54.8 | 58.6 | 61.9 |
| Qwen3-4B | 56.8 | 60.6 | 64.1 |
| Qwen3-8B | 56.8 | 61.9 | 66.0 |

Across the three scales, ULME beats the strongest baseline, LLM2VEC-GEN, by 3.3–4.1 points and LLM2Vec by 7.1–9.2 points, and the lead grows with model size, which suggests the gain does not disappear on larger backbones.

Broken down by task category, the advantage comes mainly from retrieval, summarization and pair classification, where ULME beats LLM2VEC-GEN by about 8–9, 7–8.6 and 5.3–5.7 points. The authors note that retrieval and summarization, the two biggest gains, are exactly the tasks where "the target is itself a piece of generated text". This shows that shaping the query representation with the answer helps most on such tasks. The gains are not universal, though: clustering and classification are slightly below LLM2VEC-GEN at some scales, by at most 1.5 points.

On retrieval that requires reasoning, ULME does not trade one ability for another either. On BRIGHT (nDCG@10) it beats LLM2VEC-GEN by 0.7–1.2 points, reaching 21.4 at 8B. AdvBench-IR measures whether a model retrieves harmful content, where lower is better; ULME is 20–25% lower than LLM2Vec and another 1.3–1.8 points below LLM2VEC-GEN. Both directions improve at once, which shows the better retrieval did not come at the cost of safety.

## 4. Generation results: no worse, and better on code and math

The comparison is with models fine-tuned for generation only on the same OpenThoughts-114k (Gen-only below), so any difference comes only from ULME's extra embedding objectives. On knowledge and math (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), ULME matches or beats Gen-only everywhere except Qwen3-8B MMLU, which is 0.1 lower; the clearest case is 8B GSM8K, 89.5 versus 78.6. On code it is better at every scale: HumanEval is 2.4–4.9 points higher, and 8B HumanEval+ is 67.7 versus 62.8. The authors' explanation is that making the query slots summarize in advance what the model is about to generate is especially useful for structured output like code, which can be checked by running tests. Both ULME and Gen-only sometimes score slightly below the original backbone; the authors attribute this to the distribution shift from continued training on OpenThoughts-114k, not to the joint objective.

## 5. Ablations: the three losses really do pull on each other

All ablations use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, with a 10-task MTEB-lite for embedding and MMLU and GSM8K for generation.

First, are slots needed? Without slots, taking the query's last token directly ($N=0$), MTEB-lite is 58.6, 5.2 points below the 63.8 of $N=4$, and MMLU is 2.0 points lower too. This shows the readout-position conflict from Section 1 is a real cost. One slot recovers most of the gap, $N=4$ is best, and $N=8$ dips slightly; the authors guess that a longer slot chain dilutes the gradient each slot receives.

Next, remove the losses one at a time. Without the semantic loss, MTEB-lite collapses from 63.8 to 31.2 while generation is unaffected; without the generation loss, MMLU drops 14.7 and GSM8K drops 15.8. Both are expected. There is no direct comparison in the same table with unified models such as GritLM and GEM. Turning an LLM into an embedding model is well established. E5-Mistral and NV-Embed fine-tune a causal LLM with contrastive learning and take the hidden state of the last token; LLM2Vec goes further and removes the causal mask, turning the model into a bidirectional encoder. They showed that decoder hidden states are enough for very strong embeddings, but the fine-tuned model can no longer be used for generation.

Putting retrieval and generation into one model has been tried too. GritLM trains one LLM on a contrastive loss and a language-modeling loss at the same time; another method, GEM, adds embedding ability to a generation model through extra tokens and self-supervised contrastive learning. The authors argue that these approaches unify only half the way, with gaps in two places.

The first gap is in the mechanism. GritLM switches to bidirectional attention for embedding and back to causal attention for generation, so what the embedding reads out is not on the same computation path as the hidden states used for generation.

The second gap is in the training objectives. The two losses train side by side on shared parameters without supervising each other: generation does not depend on the learned embedding, and the embedding receives no direct signal from the generation side. Sharing parameters does not by itself connect the two.

There is also a more concrete conflict about which position the embedding is read from. The usual way to embed with a causal LLM is to take the hidden state of the query's last token, but in a unified model that very position is responsible for predicting the first token of the answer. The authors call this a representation conflict: retrieval needs a sequence-level state that can be compared with other states by inner product, while language modeling needs a state that feeds the LM head and only cares about the next word, and one hidden state is asked to do both jobs.

ULME's first step is to give the embedding its own readout positions. Borrowing from latent chain-of-thought methods such as Coconut and pause tokens, it inserts N learnable slots between the query q and the answer a, so a training sample reads q∥⟨\textscemb⟩1:N​∥a, while a document is encoded as d∥⟨\textscemb⟩. The slots are ordinary positions in the causal forward pass: each slot sees the query and earlier slots, and every answer token sees all slots. The mask is not changed at all and there are no side paths; attention is causal throughout, and one forward pass yields both the embedding and the answer. The first slot (slot 0) serves as the semantic embedding, and the last slot (slot $N-1$) as the reasoning embedding.

One is a symmetric InfoNCE between the query representation and the document representation at slot 0, with in-batch negatives gathered across GPUs. The other is ordinary next-token cross-entropy, computed only on the answer. The slots themselves carry no token loss, but the slot chain sits on the causal path that produces the answer, so language-modeling gradients flow back into the slots through the answer's attention to them.

The authors point out that these two losses alone are exactly the "train side by side" setup of earlier unified models. The semantic loss only pulls slot 0 toward documents and ignores what the answer says; the generation loss is conditioned on the slots but never asks any slot to represent anything in particular.

The alignment uses a one-directional in-batch InfoNCE with a stop-gradient sg(⋅) on the answer side:
Lpred​=−log∑k​exp(⟨hq(N−1)​,sg(rqa,k​)⟩/τ)exp(⟨hq(N−1)​,sg(rqa​)⟩/τ)​
Putting the stop-gradient on the answer side is deliberate. rqa​ has seen both the query and the answer, so it holds more information than hq(N−1)​, which has seen only the query and the slots; the side with less information should reach toward the side with more. If gradients also flowed back into rqa​, the answer-side representation would be pushed toward being "easy to tell apart within the batch", interfering with the hidden states the generation loss is supervising. In effect, the answer-side representation is distilled one way into query slots that are available at inference time. The query is "how do I deduplicate a Python list while keeping order", and the training answer is a snippet using dict.fromkeys plus an explanation. The semantic loss pulls slot 0 toward the embedding of the matching document; predictive coupling pulls slot 3 toward the mean of that answer's hidden states. At inference time there is no need to generate an answer: running the query plus 4 slots is enough to read out the embedding.

papers.title: Rubric-Calibrated Preferences: Cross-Query Calibration of LLM Judgments via Item Response Theory
papers.abstract: Rerankers decide which documents users and LLMs see, yet their standard metric, nDCG, relies on human relevance labels that are costly, sparse, noisy, and discretely graded. As rerankers approach each other in quality, nDCG on these labels therefore increasingly fails to separate them. LLM judges could supply dense labels. Relative judgments within one query tell even close candidates apart, yet their scores share no scale across queries. Absolute grades share one scale but are too coarse to distinguish documents of similar relevance. We propose Rubric-Calibrated Preferences (RCP), which combine both kinds of judgment. A listwise Bradley-Terry tournament orders each query's documents, and a rubric of yes/no criteria of increasing stringency provides an absolute standard. Item Response Theory (IRT), which scores test-takers based on their answers to common questions, then uses the shared criteria to put all queries' tournament scores on one scale. RCP's retrieval metric, RCP-nDCG, replaces nDCG's discrete labels with the resulting calibrated relevance probabilities. Against blind grades from 46 external annotators, calibration raises the correlation between a query's mean score and its mean human grade from 0.538 to 0.795. The probabilities rank a useful document above a non-useful one with probability 0.910 (AUC, chance 0.5), versus 0.651 for the benchmark labels. When the annotators' grades prefer one of two rerankers and exactly one metric agrees, that metric is RCP-nDCG in 72.4% of 185 comparisons (chance about 53%). On TREC-DL, RCP-nDCG sides with NIST assessors' grades on every reranker pair that these grades separate significantly. RCP-nDCG also resolves many of nDCG's ties and separates 1.9 times as many reranker pairs on NanoBEIR. Rubric calibration thus turns relative LLM judgments into dense relevance labels that are comparable across queries and agree with human judgment.
papers.summary: As rerankers cluster in quality, nDCG on sparse discrete human labels stops separating them. LLM relative judgments split close docs but share no scale across queries; absolute grades share a scale but are too coarse. Cohere’s Rubric-Calibrated Preferences (RCP) uses IRT for cross-query calibration; RCP-nDCG replaces discrete labels: useful-vs-not AUC 0.910 (vs 0.651 for benchmark labels); among 185 comparisons where only one metric agrees, RCP-nDCG is that metric 72.4% of the time; on TREC-DL it sides with NIST grades whenever they separate. nDCG failure modes hit 45.6% of NanoBEIR and 30.7% of BRIGHT queries. ==Reranker eval must move from discrete nDCG to dense, cross-query-calibrated judgments==.

deep_reading.title: Rubric-Calibrated Preferences: Cross-Query Calibration of LLM Judgments via Item Response Theory
deep_reading.content:
Across the 14 rerankers the authors evaluated, nDCG cannot tell them apart on 45.6% of NanoBEIR queries and 30.7% of BRIGHT queries: either every reranker scores 1 (saturation), every reranker scores 0 (floor), or more than half of the pairwise comparisons tie (compression). The root cause is the human relevance labels (qrels): they are expensive and sparse, noisy, and limited to a few discrete grades, and the closer the rerankers are to each other, the worse this gets. The Cohere authors propose RCP (Rubric-Calibrated Preferences). It first has an LLM rank the documents under the same query finely with a listwise tournament, then uses a rubric of five yes/no criteria and item response theory (IRT) to put all queries on one shared ruler, yielding RCP-nDCG with continuous gains. Checked against blind ratings from 46 external annotators, ==RCP gains rank a useful document above a useless one with probability 0.910, against 0.651 for the original qrels==; on NanoBEIR, the share of reranker pairs that can be significantly separated rises from 34.1% to 63.5%.

![On three queries nDCG@10 shows saturation, floor and compression across the 14 rerankers, while RCP-nDCG@10 spreads them apart.](figs/2609.35739/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: relative judgments share no scale, and absolute judgments are too coarse

Using an LLM as a relevance judge allows labeling at scale with quality close to human. But the LLM's two ways of judging each have a weakness. The first is relative judgment, meaning pairwise or listwise comparison. It can separate very close documents under the same query, but scores from different queries share no common scale, so they cannot become graded labels, support a shared threshold, or be aggregated across queries. From the point of view of the Bradley–Terry (BT) model, scores within one set of comparisons are determined only up to an additive constant, so scores from two queries cannot be compared directly; and the judge is more decisive on some queries, so the spread of scores differs too. The second is absolute judgment, meaning assigning grades directly. It can be compared across queries, but the grades are too coarse, and many documents under the same query end up tied.

The question the authors want to answer is: can a fixed set of yes/no criteria put within-query LLM preferences on a scale shared by all queries, with results that agree with human judgment? They test this in reranker evaluation, because there is an independent human reference there, and because scores obtained this way can replace sparse, discrete, noisy qrels.

## 2. Method: the tournament sets the order, the rubric sets the scale

![RCP pipeline: Stage A scores the documents within each query with a listwise Bradley–Terry tournament, Stage B records answers to five yes/no criteria, and IRT calibration puts all queries on one scale, giving RCP-nDCG's continuous gains.](figs/2609.35739/hf2.png)

IRT was originally used for exams: from examinees' answers to the same set of questions, it places all examinees on one ability scale. RCP borrows this idea, **treating documents as examinees and the rubric's criteria as questions**. The pipeline has two stages plus a calibration step.

The first stage uses a tournament to set the order within each query. For each query's candidate set, the judge LLM looks at 10 documents at a time and gives each document in the window a score in $[-5,+5]$, with the prompt telling it this is a logit scale. The authors keep only the soft pairwise preferences within the window, $p_{ii'}=\sigma(s_i-s_{i'})$, and fit BT scores to them. Windows are scheduled over three rounds, so that comparisons concentrate where rank is still uncertain and middling documents are not dragged down by always landing in a window with clearly stronger ones.

The second stage has the judge answer absolute criteria document by document. The judge again reads 10 documents at a time, but answers five yes/no questions for each document separately, each harder than the last:

| ID | Criterion | Diagnostic question | Discrimination γ | Difficulty β |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| C1 | Topical relevance | Is the topic clearly relevant to the query's information need? | 1.17 | −2.57 |
| C2 | Useful information | Does it contain specific useful information that addresses the query? | 1.05 | −2.00 |
| C3 | Entity/detail match | Does it name and discuss the specific entities or details in the query? | 0.94 | −0.25 |
| C4 | Direct answer | Does it clearly and directly answer the query's main question? | 1.16 | 0.71 |
| C5 | In-depth treatment | Does it treat the topic in depth rather than superficially? | 0.69 | 4.12 |

(Parameters are fitted values on NanoBEIR with Qwen3.5-397B as the judge.)

The final step uses these answers to align all queries onto one scale. BT scores and the ability values of the IRT two-parameter model (2PL) are both on a logit scale, so the authors apply a linear transform to the BT score and treat it as the document's ability:

$$P(Y_{ijc}=1)=\sigma\big(\gamma_c(\tau_j\hat\theta_i^{\rm BT}+\alpha_j-\beta_c)\big)$$

Each criterion's discrimination $\gamma_c$ and difficulty $\beta_c$ are shared across all queries. Each query has its own offset $\alpha_j$, which fills in the constant BT is missing, and its own scale $\tau_j>0$, which makes "one logit of ability difference" mean the same amount of relevance difference on every query. $\alpha_j$ and $\tau_j$ are estimated from the second-stage answers for that query's documents, and the BT scores themselves stay fixed. Because $\tau_j>0$, **the order within each query is guaranteed to match the first stage** (Proposition 3.1); calibration changes only how different queries compare.

With a unified ability value, RCP-nDCG can be defined: replace nDCG's discrete gains with the discrimination-weighted "probability of passing each criterion":

$$g(\tilde\theta)=\frac{\sum_c\gamma_c\,\sigma(\gamma_c(\tilde\theta-\beta_c))}{\sum_c\gamma_c}$$

$g$ rises smoothly from 0 to 1 and climbs fastest where the rubric measures most precisely. The ideal ranking is the order from the first stage. On NanoBEIR, 79.3% of candidate documents have ability below C1's difficulty, meaning they do not even count as "topically relevant"; only about 15.6% fall between the difficulties of C1 and C4, where $g$ rises from 0.22 to 0.69, so the top candidates are separated mainly along this stretch.

An example shows what calibration changes. The query is "can aspirin prevent stroke"; two documents differ only slightly in the first stage, but both pass C1 through C3. In another query, the top document passes only C1. Looking at BT scores alone, the two queries' top documents seem equally "relevant"; after calibration, the document from the first query lands at a higher ability value and gets a higher gain.

## 3. Setup and calibration quality

The evaluation covers four groups of data: 13 NanoBEIR datasets and 12 BRIGHT tasks (both with binary qrels), TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 (graded 0–3 by NIST assessors), and 8 ViDoRe v3 corpora (three grades). To compare reranking alone, each query's candidate pool is fixed to the top 150 from RRF fusion of three retrievers (Cohere Embed v4, Octen-Embedding-8B, BM25), and positives the retrievers missed replace the lowest-ranked candidates. The 14 rerankers come from six families: Cohere, Contextual AI, Qwen3 Embedding, Voyage AI, Jina AI and ZeroEntropy. The main judge is Qwen3.5-397B, and the second judge, gpt-oss-120b, is used to check whether conclusions change with the judge.

The human reference works as follows. The authors hired 46 paid external annotators, each with at least a bachelor's degree in the subject they labeled. Each comparison is one query plus the top five from each of two rerankers; annotators rate the combined documents from both lists in random order, without seeing which list a document came from, the qrels, or any metric scores. The final analysis covers 311 comparisons and 7,080 human ratings, with three annotators per comparison.

The calibration itself is reliable, with three main pieces of evidence. First, given the calibrated ability, the answers to different criteria are only weakly correlated (mean absolute correlation 0.123, against 0.60 for raw answers), so the "questions are independent" assumption IRT requires roughly holds. Second, criterion parameters fitted on other datasets and moved to a held-out dataset predict answers with 60.6% lower cross-entropy than "guess each criterion's average pass rate", showing the parameters transfer. Third, the per-query scale $\tau_j$ varies about threefold between the 5th and 95th percentiles, which shows that queries really are on different scales and the scale term is necessary.

Calibration also brings scores closer to people. Using BT scores alone without query scaling, the calibration error (ECE) for predicting answers is 0.371; after 2PL calibration it falls to 0.017, and against human ratings the ECE is 0.054. The Spearman correlation between per-query average scores and annotators' average ratings rises from 0.538 for raw BT to 0.795 after calibration.

## 4. Main results: better separation, and the right separation

First, are the labels themselves right? Over the 2,268 documents rated blind by people, RCP gains rank a useful document (human average ≥2) above a useless one with probability 0.910, against only 0.651 for binary qrels, because about half of such document pairs share the same qrel label. Qrels disagree with people in both directions: annotators found 27.8% of documents without a positive qrel actually useful, and 37.5% of documents with a positive qrel actually useless.

Next, can it tell rerankers apart? The authors use paired t-tests to count how many of the 91 reranker pairs are significantly separated: on NanoBEIR, 34.1% with qrel-nDCG@10 and 63.5% with RCP-nDCG@10. BRIGHT, ViDoRe v3 and both years of TREC-DL also show more separation, and switching the judge to gpt-oss-120b does not change the conclusion. Count-nDCG, which uses the rubric without the tournament, separates about as many pairs as RCP-nDCG, so the extra separating power comes mainly from the rubric. But when three LLMs from other families blind-compare the ideal top tens the two produce, they prefer RCP-nDCG's version on 80.6–98.8% of queries, which shows the tournament is what resolves the finer differences.

Separating more is not enough; it has to separate correctly. In the 185 comparisons where the two metrics disagree and exactly one sides with the annotators, the one that sides correctly is RCP-nDCG 72.4% of the time, while chance is about 53% (because qrel-nDCG ties more often). When the RCP-nDCG gap reaches 0.20 or more, annotators agree with it 96.8% of the time; with the same gap, qrel-nDCG gets only 53.1%. On TREC-DL, NIST grades significantly separate only 14 reranker pairs in 2019 and 37 in 2020; RCP-nDCG agrees with NIST on all of them while also separating many more pairs.

![Rankings of the 14 rerankers on NanoBEIR under qrel-nDCG@10 (left) and RCP-nDCG@10 (right, judge Qwen3.5-397B), colored by model family.](figs/2609.35739/hf5.png)

The biggest rank change involves ZeroEntropy's rerankers. Under qrel-nDCG@10, Qwen3-Reranker-8B and Contextual v2 6B lead and ZeroEntropy's three models are at the bottom; under RCP-nDCG@10, zerank-2 and zerank-1 rise from 14th and 13th to 1st and 2nd. This raises a concern: zerank is trained on pairwise preferences from several LLMs, so RCP might simply be rewarding a signal from the same source. The authors check how people choose: in the 66 comparisons where RCP-nDCG favors zerank and qrel-nDCG favors the opponent, human annotators, who use no LLM at all, chose zerank 78.8% of the time. Removing every comparison involving zerank lowers RCP-nDCG's agreement rate from 72.4% to 68.1%, still clearly above chance. So zerank's rise is largely real, but the bias concern is not fully ruled out.

## 5. Is the rubric itself stable?

The authors tested the original rubric and 15 rewritten variants on TREC-DL. As long as the rubric does not ignore the query entirely or crowd all criteria at one end of the difficulty range, not a single significantly separated reranker pair flips. This shows RCP is not very sensitive to the rubric's wording, but the rubric must cover a range of difficulty from lenient to strict. The authors also caution that these five criteria were designed for general retrieval, and other applications may need different criteria.

## 6. Limitations and practical value

The authors acknowledge several limitations. RCP gains and human ratings both judge each document on its own and ignore redundancy between documents, which matters especially for multi-hop tasks like HotpotQA. Both measure "appears relevant", not factual correctness. The human rating questions are similar in design to the rubric. Relevance is hard to judge consistently in the first place: only 77.8% of pairs of annotators rate within one grade of each other. An LLM judge may share preferences with the rerankers being judged, so models trained on RCP signals should be checked against other labels.
