Across the 14 rerankers the authors evaluated, nDCG cannot tell them apart on 45.6% of NanoBEIR queries and 30.7% of BRIGHT queries: either every reranker scores 1 (saturation), every reranker scores 0 (floor), or more than half of the pairwise comparisons tie (compression). The root cause is the human relevance labels (qrels): they are expensive and sparse, noisy, and limited to a few discrete grades, and the closer the rerankers are to each other, the worse this gets. The Cohere authors propose RCP (Rubric-Calibrated Preferences). It first has an LLM rank the documents under the same query finely with a listwise tournament, then uses a rubric of five yes/no criteria and item response theory (IRT) to put all queries on one shared ruler, yielding RCP-nDCG with continuous gains. Checked against blind ratings from 46 external annotators, RCP gains rank a useful document above a useless one with probability 0.910, against 0.651 for the original qrels; on NanoBEIR, the share of reranker pairs that can be significantly separated rises from 34.1% to 63.5%.

1. The problem: relative judgments share no scale, and absolute judgments are too coarse

Using an LLM as a relevance judge allows labeling at scale with quality close to human. But the LLM's two ways of judging each have a weakness. The first is relative judgment, meaning pairwise or listwise comparison. It can separate very close documents under the same query, but scores from different queries share no common scale, so they cannot become graded labels, support a shared threshold, or be aggregated across queries. From the point of view of the Bradley–Terry (BT) model, scores within one set of comparisons are determined only up to an additive constant, so scores from two queries cannot be compared directly; and the judge is more decisive on some queries, so the spread of scores differs too. The second is absolute judgment, meaning assigning grades directly. It can be compared across queries, but the grades are too coarse, and many documents under the same query end up tied.

The question the authors want to answer is: can a fixed set of yes/no criteria put within-query LLM preferences on a scale shared by all queries, with results that agree with human judgment? They test this in reranker evaluation, because there is an independent human reference there, and because scores obtained this way can replace sparse, discrete, noisy qrels.

2. Method: the tournament sets the order, the rubric sets the scale

IRT was originally used for exams: from examinees' answers to the same set of questions, it places all examinees on one ability scale. RCP borrows this idea, treating documents as examinees and the rubric's criteria as questions. The pipeline has two stages plus a calibration step.

The first stage uses a tournament to set the order within each query. For each query's candidate set, the judge LLM looks at 10 documents at a time and gives each document in the window a score in $[-5,+5]$, with the prompt telling it this is a logit scale. The authors keep only the soft pairwise preferences within the window, pii′​=σ(si​−si′​), and fit BT scores to them. Windows are scheduled over three rounds, so that comparisons concentrate where rank is still uncertain and middling documents are not dragged down by always landing in a window with clearly stronger ones.

The second stage has the judge answer absolute criteria document by document. The judge again reads 10 documents at a time, but answers five yes/no questions for each document separately, each harder than the last:

IDCriterionDiagnostic questionDiscrimination γDifficulty β
C1Topical relevanceIs the topic clearly relevant to the query's information need?1.17−2.57
C2Useful informationDoes it contain specific useful information that addresses the query?1.05−2.00
C3Entity/detail matchDoes it name and discuss the specific entities or details in the query?0.94−0.25
C4Direct answerDoes it clearly and directly answer the query's main question?1.160.71
C5In-depth treatmentDoes it treat the topic in depth rather than superficially?0.694.12

(Parameters are fitted values on NanoBEIR with Qwen3.5-397B as the judge.)

The final step uses these answers to align all queries onto one scale. BT scores and the ability values of the IRT two-parameter model (2PL) are both on a logit scale, so the authors apply a linear transform to the BT score and treat it as the document's ability:
P(Yijc​=1)=σ(γc​(τj​θ^iBT​+αj​−βc​))
Each criterion's discrimination γc​ and difficulty βc​ are shared across all queries. Each query has its own offset αj​, which fills in the constant BT is missing, and its own scale τj​>0, which makes "one logit of ability difference" mean the same amount of relevance difference on every query. αj​ and τj​ are estimated from the second-stage answers for that query's documents, and the BT scores themselves stay fixed. Because τj​>0, the order within each query is guaranteed to match the first stage (Proposition 3.1); calibration changes only how different queries compare.

With a unified ability value, RCP-nDCG can be defined: replace nDCG's discrete gains with the discrimination-weighted "probability of passing each criterion":
g(θ~)=∑c​γc​∑c​γc​σ(γc​(θ~−βc​))​
g rises smoothly from 0 to 1 and climbs fastest where the rubric measures most precisely. The ideal ranking is the order from the first stage. On NanoBEIR, 79.3% of candidate documents have ability below C1's difficulty, meaning they do not even count as "topically relevant"; only about 15.6% fall between the difficulties of C1 and C4, where g rises from 0.22 to 0.69, so the top candidates are separated mainly along this stretch.

An example shows what calibration changes. The query is "can aspirin prevent stroke"; two documents differ only slightly in the first stage, but both pass C1 through C3. In another query, the top document passes only C1. Looking at BT scores alone, the two queries' top documents seem equally "relevant"; after calibration, the document from the first query lands at a higher ability value and gets a higher gain.

3. Setup and calibration quality

The evaluation covers four groups of data: 13 NanoBEIR datasets and 12 BRIGHT tasks (both with binary qrels), TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 (graded 0–3 by NIST assessors), and 8 ViDoRe v3 corpora (three grades). To compare reranking alone, each query's candidate pool is fixed to the top 150 from RRF fusion of three retrievers (Cohere Embed v4, Octen-Embedding-8B, BM25), and positives the retrievers missed replace the lowest-ranked candidates. The 14 rerankers come from six families: Cohere, Contextual AI, Qwen3 Embedding, Voyage AI, Jina AI and ZeroEntropy. The main judge is Qwen3.5-397B, and the second judge, gpt-oss-120b, is used to check whether conclusions change with the judge.

The human reference works as follows. The authors hired 46 paid external annotators, each with at least a bachelor's degree in the subject they labeled. Each comparison is one query plus the top five from each of two rerankers; annotators rate the combined documents from both lists in random order, without seeing which list a document came from, the qrels, or any metric scores. The final analysis covers 311 comparisons and 7,080 human ratings, with three annotators per comparison.

The calibration itself is reliable, with three main pieces of evidence. First, given the calibrated ability, the answers to different criteria are only weakly correlated (mean absolute correlation 0.123, against 0.60 for raw answers), so the "questions are independent" assumption IRT requires roughly holds. Second, criterion parameters fitted on other datasets and moved to a held-out dataset predict answers with 60.6% lower cross-entropy than "guess each criterion's average pass rate", showing the parameters transfer. Third, the per-query scale τj​ varies about threefold between the 5th and 95th percentiles, which shows that queries really are on different scales and the scale term is necessary.

Calibration also brings scores closer to people. Using BT scores alone without query scaling, the calibration error (ECE) for predicting answers is 0.371; after 2PL calibration it falls to 0.017, and against human ratings the ECE is 0.054. The Spearman correlation between per-query average scores and annotators' average ratings rises from 0.538 for raw BT to 0.795 after calibration.

4. Main results: better separation, and the right separation

First, are the labels themselves right? Over the 2,268 documents rated blind by people, RCP gains rank a useful document (human average ≥2) above a useless one with probability 0.910, against only 0.651 for binary qrels, because about half of such document pairs share the same qrel label. Qrels disagree with people in both directions: annotators found 27.8% of documents without a positive qrel actually useful, and 37.5% of documents with a positive qrel actually useless.

Next, can it tell rerankers apart? The authors use paired t-tests to count how many of the 91 reranker pairs are significantly separated: on NanoBEIR, 34.1% with qrel-nDCG@10 and 63.5% with RCP-nDCG@10. BRIGHT, ViDoRe v3 and both years of TREC-DL also show more separation, and switching the judge to gpt-oss-120b does not change the conclusion. Count-nDCG, which uses the rubric without the tournament, separates about as many pairs as RCP-nDCG, so the extra separating power comes mainly from the rubric. But when three LLMs from other families blind-compare the ideal top tens the two produce, they prefer RCP-nDCG's version on 80.6–98.8% of queries, which shows the tournament is what resolves the finer differences.

Separating more is not enough; it has to separate correctly. In the 185 comparisons where the two metrics disagree and exactly one sides with the annotators, the one that sides correctly is RCP-nDCG 72.4% of the time, while chance is about 53% (because qrel-nDCG ties more often). When the RCP-nDCG gap reaches 0.20 or more, annotators agree with it 96.8% of the time; with the same gap, qrel-nDCG gets only 53.1%. On TREC-DL, NIST grades significantly separate only 14 reranker pairs in 2019 and 37 in 2020; RCP-nDCG agrees with NIST on all of them while also separating many more pairs.

The biggest rank change involves ZeroEntropy's rerankers. Under qrel-nDCG@10, Qwen3-Reranker-8B and Contextual v2 6B lead and ZeroEntropy's three models are at the bottom; under RCP-nDCG@10, zerank-2 and zerank-1 rise from 14th and 13th to 1st and 2nd. This raises a concern: zerank is trained on pairwise preferences from several LLMs, so RCP might simply be rewarding a signal from the same source. The authors check how people choose: in the 66 comparisons where RCP-nDCG favors zerank and qrel-nDCG favors the opponent, human annotators, who use no LLM at all, chose zerank 78.8% of the time. Removing every comparison involving zerank lowers RCP-nDCG's agreement rate from 72.4% to 68.1%, still clearly above chance. So zerank's rise is largely real, but the bias concern is not fully ruled out.

5. Is the rubric itself stable?

The authors tested the original rubric and 15 rewritten variants on TREC-DL. As long as the rubric does not ignore the query entirely or crowd all criteria at one end of the difficulty range, not a single significantly separated reranker pair flips. This shows RCP is not very sensitive to the rubric's wording, but the rubric must cover a range of difficulty from lenient to strict. The authors also caution that these five criteria were designed for general retrieval, and other applications may need different criteria.

6. Limitations and practical value

The authors acknowledge several limitations. RCP gains and human ratings both judge each document on its own and ignore redundancy between documents, which matters especially for multi-hop tasks like HotpotQA. Both measure "appears relevant", not factual correctness. The human rating questions are similar in design to the rubric. Relevance is hard to judge consistently in the first place: only 77.8% of pairs of annotators rate within one grade of each other. An LLM judge may share preferences with the rerankers being judged, so models trained on RCP signals should be checked against other labels. There is also a conflict of interest to keep in mind: all the authors are from Cohere, Cohere paid for the human labeling, and two of the 14 rerankers and one of the three retrievers are Cohere products.

For teams working on retrieval and RAG, the value of this work is that it moves evaluation from "depending on sparse human labels" to "label the candidate pool once with an LLM, then evaluate any reranker at no further cost". The code, all judge scores and the 7,080 human ratings are open source; once the pool is labeled, any model that reorders these candidates can be scored directly without calling the judge again. The authors recommend that benchmarks report RCP-nDCG and qrel-nDCG together rather than replacing the latter with the former. Two points matter in practice. When the RCP-nDCG gap is below 0.02, agreement with people is only 47.2%, close to chance, so such gaps should be treated as ties. And if your own reranker was itself distilled from LLM preferences, keep a human-rated set for cross-checking.

papers.title: Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning for Search-State Awareness in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
papers.authors: Taewhoo Lee, Minju Song, Jungwoo Park, Chanwoong Yoon, Junha Jung, Hyeon Hwang, Sanghoon Lee, Minbyul Jeong, Jaewoo Kang
papers.abstract: Recent advances in search agents have enabled large language models to tackle complex tasks by retrieving and synthesizing external information. However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.
papers.summary: Search agents often lack search-state awareness—what is already obtained vs still missing—so they hallucinate reasoning and stop early. SARL (Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning) trains models to assess their own search state and decide whether to keep retrieving or answer. ==Stop conditions should come from self-assessed information gaps, not step budgets or a single hit==.

papers.title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Yufeng Li, Zaijing Li, Fuchen Zhang, Zongzong Wu, Ming Zhao, Fengxiao Tang
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: KG-RAG often distills continuous text into discrete symbols (semantic loss) and then clashes fragmented graphs with the continuous text LLMs were pretrained on. This paper couples graph topology with energy-driven pathfinding to preserve contextual consistency in RAG and ease structuring loss and modality mismatch. ==KG-RAG bottlenecks are often how knowledge is structured and traversed, not only retriever scores==.

papers.title: ERCLIP: Small-Data Adaptation of CLIP for Free-Length Image-Text Retrieval
papers.authors: Hoang-Bao Le, Allie Tran, Binh T. Nguyen, Liting Zhou, Cathal Gurrin
papers.abstract: CLIP's 77-token text encoder truncates detailed image descriptions. We present ERCLIP, a small-data adaptation of CLIP for long-caption image--text retrieval. During training, a long caption is split into sentences that the CLIP text encoder encodes independently; the sentence embeddings are fused by mean pooling or a gated residual Transformer scorer and receive their own contrastive loss. At inference ERCLIP is an unmodified CLIP dual encoder: test captions are still read through the 77-token window, and only training sees the full caption. We find that this fine-tuning erodes CLIP's zero-shot classification, most when the fusion output is not a combination of CLIP embeddings, and add a frozen-CLIP preservation loss on the image and short-caption embeddings. With 20k pairs and one epoch, ERCLIP improves long-caption R@1 over CLIP by 6.5--11.2 points, closing 62--77% of the gap to LongCLIP with 2% of its long captions. Preservation recovers 1.5--2.1 ImageNet zero-shot points (30--42% of the loss) and adds up to 2.4 points of COCO image-to-text R@1, at no inference cost.
papers.summary: CLIP’s 77-token text encoder truncates long captions. ERCLIP is a small-data adaptation: at train time long captions are sentence-encoded then fused by mean pool or a gated residual Transformer scorer with their own contrastive loss; at inference it is an unmodified dual encoder still reading the 77-token window. It gains 6.5–11.2 points over base CLIP and closes 62–77% of the gap to Long-CLIP. ==Long captions need not change the inference encoder—inject sentence-level signal at train time==.

papers.title: FlexVDR: Learning to Allocate Matryoshka Representation Budgets for Visual Document Retrieval
papers.authors: Haowen Xiang, Yibo Yan, Xin Zou, Shuliang Liu, Yi Cao, Mingdong Ou, Xuming Hu
papers.abstract: Visual document retrieval relies on rich multi-vector representations to capture fine-grained evidence in document pages, but encoding and matching these representations can be computationally expensive. Existing compression and elastic representation methods expose smaller configurations, yet making multiple budgets available does not determine which configuration a query should use. The allocation decision must estimate the retrieval value of alternative representations before incurring their full computation, while accommodating different resource preferences. We introduce FlexVDR, a framework for query-adaptive budget allocation within a single retriever. We construct a joint family of routes over encoder depth, embedding width, and token count. Retrieval supervision and distillation train the compact routes, while a native bypass preserves the full-budget reference. A Budget Allocator predicts route-specific retrieval utility from early query features and combines these predictions with a configurable resource preference to select a route. Experiments across five backbones on ViDoRe V1, V2, and V3 public show that FlexVDR retains much of the native retrieval quality while selecting compact routes for individual queries. A configurable resource preference allows the same retriever to adjust its computation without retraining or switching models.
papers.summary: Visual document retrieval needs rich multi-vector page evidence, so encode/match is expensive. Compression and elastic reps expose many budgets but do not say which budget a query should use. FlexVDR learns to estimate retrieval value of alternative Matryoshka representation budgets before paying full compute, then allocates per query. ==Elastic representations matter when you allocate budget per query, not when you only expose configs==.

papers.title: Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Efficient Visual Document Retrieval
papers.authors: Hoyeon Shin, Jeongyeon Kim, Yeong Jun Koh, Yeoneung Kim, Hanul Kim
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models(VLMs)have advanced Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) by enabling OCR-free, multi-vector representations. However, these models generate excessive tokens to preserve dense visual details, which severely limits retrieval scalability. Existing compression methods mitigate this overhead but rely on isolated heuristics that fail to balance token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage capacity. We propose a visual token compression framework formulated as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem. Our approach unifies these three objectives into a single alternating optimization process. Furthermore, we theoretically show that minimizing the transport cost upper-bounds the MaxSim retrieval error, ensuring ranking stability. Extensive experiments on the ViDoRe V1 and V3 benchmarks demonstrate that our method preserves fine-grained document semantics and improves the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off over state-of-the-art base-lines. Code is available at https://github.com/shhhhhyy/Unbalanced-Optimal-Transport-for-EVDR.
papers.summary: OCR-free VLM visual document retrieval emits too many tokens for scale; heuristic compressors struggle to balance importance, semantic redundancy and coverage. This paper casts visual token compression as unbalanced optimal transport (UOT), unifying those three under one objective while keeping retrieval quality. ==Spend VDR token budget as a transport problem once, not as a pile of heuristics==.
